posts.text:
An AI agent can install a package from PyPI, then immediately start running code nobody reviewed.

And in many sandbox designs, that code can inherit the same network access the installer needed.

That bothered me when I started looking more closely at how sandbox networking is usually handled.

Setup might need PyPI, a Git host, and a few external services.
Execution might need one internal API.

But if the network policy is set once when the sandbox starts, those permissions can stick around long after setup is finished.

The agent still works. Nothing crashes. Nothing looks obviously wrong.

The security gap is simply that the permission lasts longer than the task that required it.

While digging into this, I found a pattern I think is much cleaner with Tensorlake:

You can replace the network policy on a running sandbox without rebuilding it.

So the same sandbox can move through something like:
Install → broad access
Execute → minimal access
Sealed → no egress

The policy replacement is atomic, so there isn't a gap between removing the old rules and applying the new ones.

That changes the way I think about sandbox permissions:

The sandbox can stay alive. The permissions don't have to. 
Permission lifetime should track trust level, not sandbox lifetime.

I wrote up a detailed guide,and published it in Towards AI, Inc.
Link in the comments.

I was editing one of my YouTube videos recently and ran into a stupidly annoying problem.

I just wanted to remove all the unnecessary silences from the video.

But because I didn’t have a premium CapCut plan, doing it manually meant sitting there, finding every pause, cutting it, checking the edit, and repeating the same thing over and over.

So I searched for a tool that could do it automatically.

I found plenty.

Then came the catch:
- Some added watermarks.
- Some were paid.
- Some required an account.
- Some uploaded the entire video to the cloud.

None of them worked the way I wanted.

So I ended up doing what I usually do when I can't find the tool I need:
I built it.

I made AutoSilenceCut — a free, no-signup tool that processes your video directly in the browser and automatically removes unnecessary silence.

And honestly, it turned out much better than I expected.

What used to be a tedious editing task became something I could do in a few clicks.

That's exactly the kind of tool I wanted to exist.

So I built it for myself, and I'm putting it out there for everyone else who has had the same problem.

Try it here: https://lnkd.in/dXTEMUev

If you try it, I'd genuinely like to know what feels useful, what doesn't, and what you'd change.

If you want any improvements or changes or if you find any bugs,do let me know.

The optimization that made Tensorlake’s sandbox networking faster wasn’t the one I expected.

The team initially thought Kernel Transport Layer Security (kTLS) would be the big win.

It made sense. kTLS can move TLS record processing into the kernel, and with splice(2), it can avoid the usual userspace staging path for the payload.

But they did something more useful than just comparing the old system with the new one.

They measured the changes separately.
First, they removed the L7 reverse proxy and replaced it with an L4 forwarder, but still used a normal userspace copy.

Then they added kTLS + splice(2).

The result was surprisingly clear:
1.12 GB/s → 2.07 GB/s → 2.50 GB/s

And CPU usage went from:
0.90 → 0.50 → 0.49 CPU-s/GB

So the flashy optimization, kTLS, wasn't responsible for most of the CPU savings. The bigger win came from removing a layer that was parsing and buffering traffic it never actually needed to understand.

That distinction stuck with me.

When two optimizations ship together, we naturally give the interesting one the credit.

But sometimes the biggest performance improvement is much less exciting:

Delete the work you never needed to do.

The interesting part of Tensorlake's rebuild isn't just kTLS.

It's the methodology: isolate each architectural change, measure it independently, and only then decide what actually moved the numbers.

I broke down the architecture, the staged benchmarks, and when moving from L7 to L4 actually makes sense in my latest piece for Towards AI, Inc.

It made me wonder: how often do we optimize the interesting part of a system 
instead of first asking what work shouldn't exist at all?

Full article link in the comments.

I thought I was done ranking five AI document processing tools.

Then a fact-checking pass caught something I’d completely missed.

Rossum had been acquired by Coupa in May.

The pricing page still looked like business as usual, so I’d written the section assuming Rossum was still operating independently. I had to go back, rethink the comparison, and update the article.

And honestly, that reminded me why I don't fully trust most "Top 5 AI tools" articles.

A lot of them are basically: Open five websites → copy the feature lists → compare pricing → publish.I wanted to do something different.

So I grabbed an actual invoice and put the tools through the kind of document they’ll encounter in the real world.

Nothing exotic.Just a print shop billing a camera store.

But the invoice had the details that actually matter:Four payment checkboxes, with only one selected A 20% discount buried inside a line item

Placeholder text sitting where a careless parser could mistake it for real data
Layout information that gets messy when the document is flattened into plain text

That one document taught me more about production readiness than a dozen "99% accuracy" claims.

I compared Unstract, Reducto, Rossum, Nanonets, and Google Document AI across the things I actually care about:
-Layout preservation
-Schema automation
-Confidence validation
-Deployment flexibility
-Pricing you can realistically model

Unstract came out on top.But the interesting part isn't just the ranking. 

It's why.

I went through the pricing, capabilities, deployment options, and extraction workflows rather than simply repeating what each company's homepage says.

And yes, I also caught an acquisition that would have made the comparison outdated before it was even published.

Full breakdown in the comments.

My PS5 controller died mid swing playing Spiderman
.
The right stick started drifting on its own. Web-shots firing in random directions while my thumb wasn't even on it.

I went looking for somewhere to properly test it. 

Most tools I found do the same one thing: move the stick, watch a dot move on screen, that's it. 

Useful, but it stops right when the real question starts. Is my stick actually bad? Should I fix it or just buy a new controller? Will my hands even be comfortable with a different one?

Nobody was answering that.

So I built https://lnkd.in/gJQfy4C4 around the whole decision.

It consists of 39 tests no matter you have xbox, nintendo switch everything is available here.

It still does the basics well, drift detection, button response, trigger checks, WebHID calibration for Playstation. 

But then it goes further:

A Health Score that grades your controller 0 to 100 and gives you a printable report, instead of just numbers you have to interpret yourself.

A Fix or Replace calculator, because repairing a stick costs 4 to 12 dollars and a new controller costs 60 to 80, and most people don't know that gap exists until they've already bought a new one.

A Fit tool, if you're deciding on your next controller, that matches it to your hand size instead of guessing.

Also it consists of 13 fun games which you can play using your controller-both single player and multi player.

I shipped it today,and would love your feedback.

If your stick is drifting or you're not sure whether to fix or replace your controller, test it here:

https://lnkd.in/gJQfy4C4
